Schwannoma is a benign nerve sheath tumour composed entirely or nearly entirely of differentiated neoplastic Schwann cells.

Schwannoma is a benign nerve sheath tumour composed entirely or nearly entirely of differentiated neoplastic Schwann cells.

Related terminology

Subtype(s) (to be edited – awaiting ICD-O-4 codes and subtypes)

Ancient schwannoma; cellular schwannoma; plexiform schwannoma; epithelioid schwannoma; microcystic/reticular schwannoma

Common sites of origin are peripheral nerves in the skin and subcutaneous tissues of the head and neck or along the flexor surfaces of the extremities. Spinal intradural extramedullary examples are also common and form dumbbell tumours when growing through neural foramina, with multiple paraspinal schwannomas being commonplace in NF2-related schwannomatosis (neurofibromatosis type 2). Cranial nerve involvement is fairly common, with cerebellopontine angle tumours emanating from the vestibular division of the eighth cranial nerve encountered most often and bilateral involvement being a definitional criterion for NF2-related schwannomatosis {19545378; 38925914}. Spinal intramedullary and CNS sites are rare and genetically unique {8331403; 39713960}. Those involving viscera (such as the gastrointestinal tract) and bone are also rare {22137423; 38020582}.

Schwannomas are slow-growing tumours. They often present as asymptomatic masses or incidental findings on imaging studies; however, they may be painful, particularly in the setting of schwannomatosis. Spinal schwannomas may elicit sensory symptoms such as radicular pain and motor signs if growing intraspinally. Vestibular schwannomas often present with hearing loss and vertigo.

More than 90% of these lesions are solitary and sporadic; they may affect all ages, but the peak incidence is in the fourth to sixth decades of life. There is no known predisposition with regard to race or sex.

The etiology of most sporadic schwannomas is not known, although there is an established increased incidence associated with prior irradiation {3173432; 12381708}. There is an association with tumour predisposition syndromes in some cases (see Pathogenesis, below).

A causal relationship exists between schwannoma tumorigenesis and loss of expression of merlin (NF2, schwannomin), the growth inhibitory protein product of the NF2 tumour suppressor gene located at 22q12.2 {9403715}. NF2-inactivating mutations have been detected in approximately 50–75% of sporadic cases {8889506; 23921927; 26360373; 28409725}. Underlying genetic events are predominantly frameshift and nonsense mutations, with loss of the remaining wildtype allele on chromosome 22. Other common mutations involve the LATS1, LATS2, ARID1A, ARID1B, DDR1, and SOX10 {37436963; 40272443} genes, whereas a recurrent in-frame SH3PXD2A::HTRA1 fusion is found in roughly 10% of cases {26360373; 27723760; 34213706; 38219951}.

Multiple schwannomas are a feature of NF2-related schwannomatosis and other types of schwannomatosis (including SMARCB1-related, LZTR1-related, and chromosome 22–related schwannomatosis), each of which can also occur in mosaic or segmental forms {26851632; 27921248; 38925914}. NF2-associated schwannomas commonly present before the age of 30 years, whereas tumours usually manifest in later adulthood in other forms of schwannomatosis. Bilateral vestibular schwannoma is a hallmark of NF2-related schwannomatosis, often showing multifocal nerve involvement and a nodular microscopic growth pattern. In addition, patients with the more severe Wishart form of NF2-related schwannomatosis typically have meningiomas, which are often multiple and associated with increased morbidity and mortality. Gliomas, most frequently cervical spinal ependymoma, develop less commonly {19545378}. NF2-related schwannomatosis is inherited in an autosomal dominant manner, with 50% of cases representing new or sporadic variants.

Schwannomatosis (non–NF2-related) is characterized by the presence of multiple schwannomas, mostly (but not invariably) in the absence of vestibular nerve involvement and meningiomas. Cranial and cutaneous nerves are infrequently affected. Germline mutations of either the SMARCB1 or LZTR1 tumour suppressor gene are found in 86% of patients with familial schwannomatosis and 40% of patients with sporadic schwannomatosis {27921248}. Nevertheless, the tumorigenesis appears to be more complex given that these tumours arise from a three-hit or four-hit mechanism that involves two genes. One common pattern is a germline SMARCB1 or LZTR1 mutation followed by a somatic NF2 mutation on the same chromosome 22 and a deletion of the entire other chromosome 22, leading to biallelic inactivation of both tumour suppressor genes simultaneously (i.e. three hits). Not surprisingly, therefore, the somatic NF2 mutation often differs among schwannomas from any one patient, as well as between the schwannomas of different family members.

Recent studies have shown a strong association between VGLL3 or VGLL1 fusion and intraparenchymal CNS schwannomas {39713960}, although these same fusions may also be found in hybrid schwannoma-perineurioma in the peripheral nervous system {33649458}.

Epigenetically, schwannomas comprise two distinct groups characterized by differential methylation and expression of genes involved in nervous system / neural crest development or immunological signalling, with immune-enriched tumours showing greater macrophage and lymphocyte infiltration, vascular hyalinization, and necrosis than neural crest tumours {38216587}. Conversion from neural crest to immune-enriched schwannoma can be induced by radiotherapy {38216587}.

These tumours are mainly solitary and globoid, have a smooth surface, and measure < 100 mm in greatest dimension, except for giant schwannomas, which are mostly encountered in the lumbosacral region. Fewer than half have an evident attached nerve, which is most often small. The uninvolved nerve fascicles are often found draped over the tumour capsule. Except for those arising in CNS parenchyma, skin, viscera, and bone, the tumours are usually encapsulated. Sectioned tumours reveal firm, light-tan, glistening tissue, interrupted by areas of white/yellow xanthic change, cystic degeneration, and/or haemorrhage.

Conventional schwannoma is usually an encapsulated spindle cell tumour that is composed nearly entirely of well-differentiated Schwann cells. Schwannomas have a broad morphological range. The large majority are biphasic tumours with compact areas (Antoni A tissue) showing occasional nuclear palisading (Verocay bodies), alternating with loosely arranged foci (Antoni B tissue). Cells of Antoni A tissue possess modest eosinophilic cytoplasm; no discernible cell borders; and normochromatic, elongated, tapered nuclei. Cytoplasmic nuclear inclusions, nuclear pleomorphism, and mitotic figures may be seen. Verocay bodies take the form of parallel rows of Schwann cell nuclei separated by their aligned cell processes. Antoni B tissue commonly contains a cobweb-like network of tumour processes with collections of lipid-laden histiocytes and thick-walled, hyalinized blood vessels, at times in clusters. Foci of haemosiderin deposition consistent with previous haemorrhage and areas of cystic degeneration are not infrequent. Lymphoid aggregates are often present in a subcapsular distribution or at the periphery in unencapsulated tumours.

A minority of schwannomas deviate from the description above. Tumours of the eighth cranial nerve show predominantly Antoni A tissue, and intestinal schwannomas typically lack Antoni B tissue. The most extreme deviation is seen in the morphological subtypes (see below).

Diffuse staining for S100 in cell nuclei and cytoplasm, which is more prominent in Antoni A than in Antoni B areas, is found in all tumours and subtypes. Similarly, SOX10 immunoreactivity is usually extensive {18636017; 22495377}. Expression of GFAP is less frequent and more variable. Pericellular collagen IV stain is typically present, consistent with the presence of a continuous basement membrane. Retroperitoneal and mediastinal lesions are commonly positive for keratins because of cross-reactivity with other intermediate filaments. In contrast to the lattice-like staining pattern in neurofibromas, CD34 is commonly positive only in subcapsular areas, although a small subset of cases show more extensive positivity. Staining for NFP is helpful in identifying entrapped intratumoural axons, found in many sporadic schwannomas, albeit most often at their periphery {17721192}. EMA highlights perineurial cells in the capsule, if present.

Ancient schwannoma

This subtype differs from the conventional schwannoma only by its presence of scattered atypical to bizarre-appearing nuclei, a feature that is often considered degenerative. Such cases may show extensive hyalinization or central ischaemic changes.

Cellular schwannoma

This subtype is composed exclusively or predominantly of Antoni A tissue and is devoid of Verocay bodies. The tumours most commonly involve large nerves and nerve plexuses at paravertebral sites, mediastinum, retroperitoneum, and pelvis {7337161; 2400975; 25189642}. Cranial nerves can rarely be affected {19200646; 31379028}. In addition to being closely packed, the cells are not uncommonly hyperchromatic and mitotically active. Small areas of microscopic necrosis may be seen. These features may raise concern for malignant peripheral nerve sheath tumour (MPNST); however, the presence of conventional features of schwannoma, including encapsulation, subcapsular lymphocytes, hyalinized blood vessels, and Schwannian whorls, aids in this distinction. Cellular schwannoma shows Ki-67 labelling hotspots (rather than diffuse increases), with an index still < 20%, and retained expression of both p16 and H3K27me3 {25189642}. Tumour erosion of nearby bone may occur.

Plexiform schwannoma

These conventional or cellular subtypes often arise in skin or subcutaneous tissue, growing as thinly encapsulated plexiform or multinodular tumours {18439936; 3096870}. More infrequently, these tumours can occur in the deep soft tissues {16006798}. The tumours come to clinical attention earlier in life, often in childhood and even at birth {14508393}, with some predilection for the trunk and head and neck region. Most are sporadic, but they have also been occasionally reported in patients with schwannomatosis (including NF2-related schwannomatosis). Biphasic plexiform schwannomas are more readily identified pathologically than plexiform cellular examples. The latter are composed of solid nodules separated by thin fibrous bands or of more-infiltrative nodules with entrapped axons. The tumours generally differ from the conventional schwannoma in their absence of a well-formed capsule and thick-walled vessels.

Epithelioid schwannoma

Most epithelioid schwannomas are sporadic, although some may be multiple and/or arise in the setting of non–NF2-related schwannomatosis {26752543; 28368924}. Tumours show multilobulated growth of epithelioid cells, arranged singly or in nests within a myxoid and/or hyalinized stroma. Tumour cells show eosinophilic cytoplasm and uniform, round nuclei with small or inconspicuous nucleoli, occasionally with pseudoinclusions. Conventional areas of spindled morphology, Antoni A or Antoni B tissue, and vessels with hyalinized walls may be present. Loss of SMARCB1 expression is observed in approximately 40% of cases, and such cases are associated with SMARCB1 inactivation {28368924; 30864974}. Some examples show increased cytological atypia, and rare examples show malignant transformation to epithelioid MPNST.

Microcystic/reticular schwannoma

This is the rarest subtype of schwannoma, and tumours seem to preferentially arise in visceral sites, most commonly in the gastrointestinal tract {18520439} and skin {40206896}. Most lesions are encapsulated, except in visceral sites. Microscopically, tumours are characterized by a microcyst-rich network of interconnected bland spindle cells with eosinophilic cytoplasm, associated with a myxoid, fibrillary, and/or hyalinized collagenous stroma. Antoni A tissue is frequent, and tumours show strong and extensive S100 and SOX10 expression. However, conventional features of hyalinized blood vessels, foamy histiocytes, and Verocay bodies are generally absent.

Other patterns

Although most syndrome-associated schwannomas are not histologically distinguishable from their sporadic counterparts, several clinicopathological clues may indicate a setting of schwannomatosis or NF2-related schwannomatosis: young patient age, multiple tumours, extensive longitudinal involvement of a nerve, discontinuous or multinodular growth pattern, and a mosaic SMARCB1 immunostaining pattern defined by an admixture of positive and negative nuclei {18422762; 28365909}. Some schwannomas feature predominantly small blue round cells with or without structures resembling Homer Wright rosettes or giant rosettes surrounding collagen fibres resembling those of low-grade fibromyxoid sarcoma. These cases are often referred to as neuroblastoma-like, although they lack increased proliferative activity and show a typical schwannoma immunoprofile {30582192}. Another rare pitfall is a schwannoma with neuromelanin-like pigment accumulation that is positive on Fontana–Masson staining. Nevertheless, the histology is otherwise typical of schwannoma, and the tumour cells are negative for more-specific melanocytic markers, such as HMB45 {10792787}; therefore, these should not be equated with the more aggressive and Carney complex / PRKAR1A–associated malignant melanotic nerve sheath tumour (previously termed melanotic schwannoma).

Aspirated material shows moderate to high cellularity with cohesive branching and anastomosing fish net–like fascicular or syncytial tissue fragments consisting of spindle cells with poorly defined cytoplasm in a variably collagenous or myxoid matrix. Spindle cells have elongated wavy nuclei and common intranuclear pseudoinclusions and may be seen singly in the clean background. Hyalinized thick-walled vessels are commonly seen in the tissue fragments, which usually do not show Antoni A and B regions. Degenerative hyperchromatic smudge-like chromatin can be seen {16680779; 16850489; 25641870; 36650522}.

Essential: a benign tumour composed almost entirely of Schwann cells, displaying various architectural patterns as described above.

Desirable: diffuse immunoreactivity for S100 and SOX10.

Schwannomas are benign tumours and do not usually recur if treated by gross total resection. Cellular and plexiform examples are least amenable to total removal and sometimes can only be debulked. Malignant transformation of conventional schwannoma is exceptionally rare. In the small number of cases reported to date, it has most often taken the form of epithelioid MPNST {8067509; 11145248; 22082606}. Less common examples feature foci of conventional MPNST, primitive tumour cells, rhabdomyosarcoma, and/or angiosarcoma {8067509; 8898847; 11145248; 12766593; 22082606; 27512546}.
